message:
QUESTION:
Under the council's affordability rule, can a median-income household in the city afford to buy the median house, or to rent a median 2-bedroom flat?

DATA:
City housing affordability, 2025.

- Median house price: £320,000. Lower-quartile house price: £230,000.
- Median gross household income: £40,000 a year. Median take-home (net) household income: £2,700 a month.
- Over the past year, median house prices rose 6% and median household incomes rose 3%.
- First-time-buyer assumptions: 10% deposit, 25-year capital-repayment mortgage at 5.0% fixed interest.
  - Monthly repayment on a £288,000 loan (median house): £1,684.
  - Monthly repayment on a £207,000 loan (lower-quartile house): £1,210.
- Median rent, 2-bedroom flat: £1,150 a month.
- Council affordability rule: housing costs are 'affordable' if they take no more than 35% of net (take-home) household income.
- Repayment figures use the standard repayment-mortgage formula and exclude insurance and maintenance. Rents exclude bills.
- Income figures cover all household types in the city.
- The council applies the 35% rule to both renting and buying.
- No data are available on planning permissions, housing supply, or who is buying homes in the city.

<analysis>
# Is the city affordable for a median household?

**Short answer: No, on either tenure.** Under the council's 35%-of-net-income rule, a median-income household can afford neither the median house nor a median 2-bedroom rent. Even a lower-quartile house fails the test.

**Scope.** This note applies the council's rule to a household on the median income, using the figures supplied. Mortgage repayments exclude insurance and maintenance, and rents exclude bills, so real housing costs will be somewhat higher than shown.

**The threshold.** Median take-home household income is £2,700 a month. 35% of that is **£945 a month**. This is the most a median household can spend on housing under the rule.

## Buying

| | Median house | Lower-quartile house |
|---|---|---|
| Price | £320,000 | £230,000 |
| 10% deposit | £32,000 | £23,000 |
| Loan | £288,000 | £207,000 |
| Monthly repayment (25 yrs, 5.0%) | £1,684 | £1,210 |
| Share of net income (£2,700) | **62%** | **45%** |
| Passes 35% test? | No | No |

- The median-house repayment is £739 a month above the £945 threshold, close to double the affordable level. Over the full term, repayments total about £505,000.
- Under the same mortgage terms, £945 a month would service a loan of about £162,000. With a 10% deposit, that means a house price of roughly **£180,000**, well below even the lower-quartile price.
- The deposit is a separate barrier. £32,000 is nearly 12 months of the household's entire take-home income.

## Renting

The median 2-bedroom rent is £1,150 a month. That is **43% of take-home income** (£1,150 / £2,700), which is above the 35% threshold, so it **fails** the council's test. It is £205 a month above the £945 limit.

(If rent were measured against gross monthly income of £3,333, it would come to 34.5% and appear to just pass. But the council's rule is defined on net income and applies to renting as well as buying, so gross income is not the correct basis.)

Renting is still much cheaper each month than buying (£1,150 against £1,684). It also needs no deposit, so it is the less unaffordable option. It does not, however, meet the council's definition of affordable.

## Price-to-income ratio and trend

- The median house price is **8.0 times** median gross household income (£320,000 / £40,000). This ratio is not part of the council's rule, but it is a widely used summary measure. Ratios this high are generally regarded as severely unaffordable.
- **Affordability worsened over the past year.** House prices rose 6% while incomes rose only 3%. Backing out last year's figures (about £302,000 and £38,800) gives a ratio of about 7.8, so it has risen to 8.0 in a year. Only one year of change is available, so these data cannot show whether this is a long-term trend.

## Causes

The data do not explain *why* prices are high relative to incomes. There is no information on planning permissions, housing supply, population or who is buying homes. Supply constraints, interest rates, investor or second-home demand and local labour-market factors are all possible explanations. Identifying the cause would need further data.

## Conclusions

1. **Buying the median house is unaffordable** for a median household. The repayment takes 62% of take-home pay against a 35% limit. A lower-quartile house also fails, at 45%. The rule would be met only at a price of around £180,000.
2. **Renting a median 2-bedroom flat is also unaffordable** under the council's rule, at 43% of take-home pay. It is the less costly option and needs no deposit.
3. **The position worsened over the last year**, as prices grew twice as fast as incomes.
4. The data do not support any particular policy remedy. Choosing one requires evidence on causes.

**Caveats.** These figures describe a household on exactly the median income. The income figures cover all household types, including single-person households, which may not want or need a 2-bedroom flat or a house. Households with two earners or existing equity will be better placed, and single-earner households with children worse placed. Excluded costs (bills, insurance, maintenance) would push every percentage above higher.

---

### Main corrections to the draft

- **Buying share was wrong:** £1,684 / £2,700 is 62%, not 52%.
- **Renting used the wrong income basis:** it divided by gross income (£3,333). On the council's net-income basis, rent is 43%, so it is unaffordable, not "just affordable".
- **Trend was misread:** incomes rose 3%, not 6%, so the price-to-income ratio worsened rather than staying stable. The "long-standing / structural" inference also isn't supported by one year of data.
- **Unsupported causal claim removed:** the data contain nothing on planning or supply, so the planning-restrictions explanation and the policy recommendation were dropped.
- **Added** the £945 affordability threshold and the maximum affordable price (about £180,000) to make the gap concrete.
</analysis>

Please review this analysis.
response:
# Review: the analysis is sound, with a few small fixes needed

I recomputed every figure. The arithmetic is correct and the conclusions follow from the data. **Neither buying nor renting passes the council's 35% rule for a median-income household.**

## Figures checked

| Claim | Check | OK? |
|---|---|---|
| Threshold £945 | 0.35 × £2,700 | ✓ |
| Repayment £1,684 / £1,210 | Annuity formula, 5%/12, 300 months gives £1,683.6 / £1,210.1 | ✓ |
| 62% / 45% of net income | 1,684/2,700 = 62.4%; 1,210/2,700 = 44.8% | ✓ |
| £739 over threshold | 1,684 − 945 | ✓ |
| Total repaid ≈ £505,000 | 1,684 × 300 = £505,200 | ✓ |
| Max loan ≈ £162k, price ≈ £180k | 945 / 0.005846 = £161,650; ÷ 0.9 = £179,600 | ✓ |
| Deposit ≈ 12 months' net pay | 32,000 / 2,700 = 11.9 | ✓ |
| Rent 43%, £205 over | 1,150/2,700 = 42.6% | ✓ |
| Gross-basis rent 34.5% | 1,150 / 3,333 | ✓ |
| Price-to-income 8.0, prior year ≈ 7.8 | 320/40; 301.9/38.8 = 7.77 | ✓ |

The answer to the question is correct. The analysis uses the right income basis (net) and states its limits clearly.

## Issues to fix

1. **"Renting needs no deposit" is inaccurate.** Renting usually needs a tenancy deposit, though a much smaller one (in England, capped at 5 weeks' rent, about £1,300 here). Say "no purchase deposit" or "only a small tenancy deposit".

2. **"Close to double the affordable level" overstates the gap.** £1,684 / £945 is 1.78×. "Nearly 80% above" is more precise.

3. **"Ratios this high are generally regarded as severely unaffordable"** relies on an outside benchmark the data don't contain. It also contrasts with the careful refusal to go beyond the data elsewhere. Either cite the benchmark (e.g. Demographia's "above 5.0" category) or soften it to "very high by common benchmarks".

4. **Remove the "Main corrections to the draft" section from the deliverable.** It refers to a draft the reader hasn't seen. It is useful as a change log for the author, but it should be kept separate from the analysis itself.

5. **The buy-versus-rent comparison could note what it leaves out.** Saying renting is "less unaffordable" compares monthly cash costs only. Mortgage repayments build equity and rent does not. One clause would prevent misreading. Optionally, also note that a renting household paying 43% of take-home pay would struggle to save the £32,000 deposit, which links the two barriers.

## Minor points, optional

- "Single-earner households with children worse placed" is a reasonable assumption but goes beyond the data. Frame it as "likely".
- The caveat about the all-household-types income figure is good. It could be moved nearer the top, because it is the main limitation on how far the conclusion generalises.

**Verdict:** the analysis is ready to use after the five small edits above. None of them changes the conclusions.
